title: Wheat and weeds (Matthew 13:24–43)
hookLine: pull the weeds too early and the good crop comes up too
tomorrow: should you keep the old thing, or swap it for the new one?

cards: Weed a spring garden too early and you learn fast: the young tomato and the weed look a lot alike, and their roots are already tangled. Pull one and the other comes up in your fist.

Jesus tells a farm story with that exact problem. "But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way." When the blades come up, there are the weeds, all through the field.
The servants have a plan ready: shall we go and pull them up?

teach.b: The owner says no. "Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest." Notice his reason.
He never says the weeds are fine.
He says the pulling would do damage.

Later, in a house, the disciples ask what it means, and he names each piece: the field is the world, the good seed the children of the kingdom, the tares the children of the wicked one, and "the reapers are the angels."

teach.h: THE SERVANTS AREN'T ON THE LIST.
teach.b: Read the list again and look for the servants. They aren't on it. The ones most eager to sort the field are never handed the job.
The sorting belongs to the harvest, and to someone else.
And the story ends on light, not on weeds: "Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father."

how: Some Christians point to the wheat and the tares when they speak about patience with people inside and outside the church, and about leaving final judgment to God.

o: a field where good and bad grow tangled
a harvest feast held at the end of summer
a farm law about which crops to plant

games.q: one field, two crops — tap the pairs.
p: sown by an enemy while men slept

s: the owner says the weeds are fine
he never says that. he says pulling them now would root up the wheat too.
the servants are given the job of sorting at the harvest
in Jesus' explanation the reapers are the angels; the servants aren't on the list.
the parable ends with the righteous shining like the sun
"Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father."

games.q: a new volunteer at the food pantry is curt with everyone. after one Saturday, a longtime helper wants them gone. what fits the owner's answer?
o: remove them now, before the attitude spreads.
never say a word, even if they hurt someone.
give it time; you might be pulling up wheat.
games.why: the owner doesn't call weeds fine; he says early pulling roots up wheat too. let both grow together until the harvest.

practice: Close your eyes, and bring to mind one person you've already sorted into the weeds. Don't excuse anything they did, and don't stand closer to harm; just hand the final verdict back.
Breathe, and let both grow in the field a while longer.

wordCard.voice: Wheat and weeds. One field, two crops tangled at the root, and an owner who says the sorting can wait for the harvest.

orig.note: Greek for the weeds in Matthew 13:25, tares in the King James.

carryVoice: For this week's end: let both grow, and leave the harvest to the one who owns the field. That's the week.
